pocket_provenance.source: GB/T 22751-2008, table 1, Chinese table row (original scanned page checked)
pocket_provenance.corner_mouth: 84 +/- 1 mm historical national-standard reference; current prototype uses 84 mm minimum throat width
pocket_provenance.side_mouth: 86 +/- 1 mm historical national-standard reference; current prototype uses 86 mm minimum throat width
pocket_provenance.jaw_radius: Corner R30 mm engineering approximation, not a measured standard radius. C1 tangent to flat rail and channel.
pocket_provenance.side_jaw_radius: Side R40 mm engineering approximation, not a measured standard radius. Distinct from corner jaws.
pocket_provenance.shelf_depth: Corner support front tangent remains 10 mm behind the flared entrance. Side pockets now use the independent signed side_fall_front_offset. Neither is a measured slate shelf or 3-D falling model.
pocket_provenance.side_fall_front_offset: Engineering revision after review: side support front is 15 mm inward of the straight cushion nose (positive means outward). With R47 mm this moves both side fall centres inward 25 mm, from 57 to 32 mm outward. Selected as a bounded geometry adjustment below half a ball diameter; NOT a manufacturer standard, photo measurement or calibrated real-table value. The circular slate edge is independent of the unchanged rubber jaws and 86 mm throat.
pocket_provenance.support_curve: CN2311752Y distinguishes circular lower fall lines from cushion-jaw curves. Slate of China describes separate rounded corner/side cut-outs machined to customer drawings. Corner fall R45 mm and side fall R47 mm are explicit engineering approximations, not published standard or manufacturer measurements. Circle interior with jaw clearance is the absorbing region; renderer uses the identical circles.
pocket_provenance.jaw_extension: 90 mm experimental channel; unchanged. Slate cut, metal pocket body and rubber nose radii are not interchangeable.
pocket_provenance.geometry: Four identical mirrored corner pockets and two identical mirrored side pockets. Circles meet flat noses and channels tangentially; rendering and collision use the same surfaces.

cue_provenance: Engineering defaults for a horizontal point impulse; effective cue mass, tip restitution and legal disk are uncalibrated. Positive tip_x is the shooter's right; positive tip_y is up. No cue squirt, elevation, jumping or masse model. Speed range revised to 0–5 m/s: 50% center hit launches about 3.30 m/s (7.4 mph), near Alciatore TP B.6 medium 7 mph; 75% about 4.95 m/s (11.1 mph), near fast 12 mph. This is a documented UI mapping, not a measured human stroke calibration. Source: https://drdavepoolinfo.com/technical_proofs/new/TP_B-6.pdf Direct cue-speed evidence and sample limits are in stroke_reference; 5 m/s is a conservative app cap near a measured break-shot sample, not the maximum possible human cue speed.

stroke_reference.definition: Cue-tip / cue velocity immediately before ball impact, not cue-ball speed. Software bands are descriptive, not population percentiles.
stroke_reference.max_speed_basis: 5.0 m/s conservative application cap, close to the 4.7 +/- 0.5 m/s break-shot sample; not an absolute human maximum. No increase to manufacture travel distance.

sources.title: Kong et al., ISB/JSB 2023, P01-30, printed page 614
sources.sample: 22 male active cue-sports players, mean experience 5.8 years, 8 nine-ball breaks each, 250 Hz motion capture

sources.title: Kornfeind et al. 2015, Procedia Engineering 112:540-545
sources.sample: 20 elite pool players, 18 follow/draw/stop/break tasks; discussion gives maximal follow/draw cue velocity about 4.5 m/s

sources.title: Song et al., A biomechanical analysis of the upper limb on different snooker batting techniques, Table 2
sources.sample: 8 professional snooker players; prescribed follow/draw placement tasks, not all ordinary shots

stroke_reference.interpretation: Together these support practising at cue speeds around 1-3 m/s, stronger draw at 3-4.5 m/s, and a capped break-like endpoint near 5 m/s. These are software practice bands, not experimentally established universal limits.
